title: NASA Awards ~$600M in CLPS Phase One Lander Contracts to Astrobotic, Firefly, Intuitive Machines
detail: NASA announced four new Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) Phase One Moon Base delivery contracts on June 30, 2026, totaling nearly $600 million: Astrobotic received $297.9 million for two Peregrine-class deliveries, Firefly Aerospace received $144.2 million for one Blue Ghost delivery, and Intuitive Machines received $148.3 million for one Nova-C delivery, all targeting late 2028. Each mission will carry three flight-proven payloads: SCALPSS (a four-camera stereo system measuring engine-plume/lunar-dust interaction), a laser retroreflector array (LRA) for orbital navigation, and LETS, a radiation-monitoring spectrometer for astronaut safety planning. The awards came the same day responses were due on NASA's CLPS 2.0 request for proposals. NASA Associate Administrator Lori Glaze said the awards "demonstrate our commitment to accelerating our effort to build a long-term presence on the lunar surface," while Moon Base Acting Director Ryan Stephan said "accelerating our Moon mission ordering cadence enables us to move quickly to learn, iterate, and improve."

title: Blue Origin Outlines New Glenn Return-to-Flight Logistics; Blue Moon Mk1 Slips to Early 2027
detail: Blue Origin detailed its New Glenn return-to-flight plan on June 30, 2026, following the May 28 hotfire explosion at LC-36. The company is shifting from a pure horizontal integration model to a 'horizontal/vertical hybrid CONOPS': the first and second stages will be integrated horizontally in the facility adjacent to LC-36A, then a crane will hoist the assembled rocket into vertical orientation at the pad — bypassing reconstruction of the destroyed transporter-erector. CEO Dave Limp said early root-cause analysis "points to the aft section of the first stage," with specifics about the BE-4 engines still under review. The Blue Moon Mark 1 uncrewed lunar lander (Endurance) has slipped from late summer 2026 to early 2027 as a result. NASA is exploring contingency options, including potentially flying the intact Mark 1 lander on an alternative rocket if New Glenn timelines slip further, given the lander's relevance to the Blue Moon Mk2 HLS vehicle NASA is counting on for Artemis III/IV dock demonstrations.
